about: The original brief, item by item, and how each item was met. Every quote is verbatim from section 1 of docs/REBUILD-BRIEF.md. reqs name rows of docs/REQUIREMENTS.md, from which the tests, mutations and status are taken. A test keeps this honest: a 'met' item may link only to requirements that are Done, a 'partly' or 'open' item must say what is missing, and every quote, file and requirement named here must exist.

sections.title: The scenario
sections.blurb: What the brief says the CMS sends, and the corner cases it asks to be treated appropriately.

items.quote: Add → new entities are being created.
items.how: A publish for an id the service has never seen creates the entity: published, at the event's version, with the payload stored whole and never merged. The sample schema has no separate 'add' type, so a first publish is the add.

items.quote: Update → an existing entity was successfully changed.
items.how: A publish with a higher version replaces version, payload and checksum. A lower version is ignored as stale and an exact repeat as a duplicate. The end state is the same whatever order events arrive in or however batches are split; that is checked against an independent oracle on shuffled timelines.

live.label: Try the out-of-order and replay scenarios

items.quote: Delete → an entity was removed or unpublished. Please note that unpublishing the entity does not remove it from the CMS, but disables it.
items.how: Treated as the two different events the sample schema shows. Delete removes the entity and its payload for good, leaving only a payload-free tombstone that stops older events bringing it back. UnPublish keeps the row and payload and hides it from users, as the brief says the CMS merely disables it.

items.quote: An “unpublish” event will contain the entity fields, as well as the version that is being unpublished.
items.how: An unPublish carries a version and a payload and is validated like a publish. One newer than what is stored overwrites payload and version and marks the entity unpublished; an older one is ignored. At the same version and instant, unPublish beats publish whichever arrives first.

items.quote: However, since there was no published version before that, you do no longer have the latest version in your database. Please also treat this corner case appropriately!
items.how: An unPublish for an id never seen creates the entity from the unPublish's own payload, unpublished, so the latest version is not lost: X, then X+1 unpublished with nothing published between, ends as an unpublished entity at X+1. It is pinned by a test and by a deliberate-defect check that the test must catch.

live.label: Send an unPublish for a new id

items.quote: Since the system does not provide any information about which data is of the said tier, you have to assume all data is restricted.
items.how: Everything is treated as confidential and fails closed. A fallback policy requires sign-in for every route (only /health is open); a test lists every mapped route and fails if one has no row in the role matrix. Responses are never cached, and no payload, password or Authorization header is ever logged. Nothing is served publicly.

items.quote: Please authenticate your endpoints so that only allowed users can access the REST API. You can use the same basic auth used for the CMS, but the users should be different. One is an organization request (the CMS sending updates), the other is user requests.
items.how: Basic authentication with separate accounts for separate jobs: the CMS account (it writes, and cannot read), users (they read) and admins (they read everything and override). The CMS cannot read the API and users cannot ingest. Credentials are compared in constant time and repeated failed sign-ins from one address are throttled.

live.label: Run the matrix and the sign-in cases

sections.title: 1. Data ingestion layer
sections.blurb: The webhook, its security, and the batch format.

items.quote: Expose a webhook endpoint: /cms/events
items.how: POST /cms/events takes a JSON array of events and answers 202 only once the whole batch is safely stored. Only the CMS account may call it.

items.quote: Secure your endpoint using Basic Authentication.
items.how: A Basic authentication handler guards the webhook; a wrong or missing credential is 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge, and a valid user or admin is 403. Because Basic sends the password with every request, Production enables HTTPS redirection and HSTS and the docs say Basic is only safe over TLS.

items.quote: Username: feel free to use any string with a length of 10 to 20 characters.
items.how: The CMS username is validated at startup: the service refuses to start, naming the setting, if it is not 10 to 20 characters. The development account, cms-ingest-svc, is 14.

items.quote: Password: random guid.
items.how: Every CMS password must parse as a GUID, checked at startup, and several may be active so one can be rotated without downtime. In Development the service generates random GUID passwords into a git-ignored file the first time it runs; no credential is committed.

items.quote: Accept batch events. The first version added is version 1, and you can get multiple revisions per entity.
items.how: Batches of up to 500 events are accepted. A version is an integer of at least 1 and gaps are allowed. Each event in a batch is validated and answered on its own, so one bad event never blocks its neighbours.

items.quote: Schema example below:
items.how: All three event types and their fields are supported as in the example. The sample JSON itself is not valid JSON (typographic quotes and a trailing comma), so it was reproduced as given and the treatment decided in the design: parsing is strict, invalid JSON is a 400, and real traffic is assumed to be valid JSON.

items.quote: Incoming data must be validated and sanitized.
items.how: Validated: every rule has a stable reason code (missing id, invalid version, payload too large, timestamp in the future and so on) with an input just inside and just outside each limit. Sanitised means normalised, never altered: ids are trimmed, timestamps become UTC, payloads are stored in a compact canonical form, control characters in ids are rejected and untrusted text is bounded. Values are deliberately not HTML-escaped; escaping belongs to whoever renders them.

items.quote: Deleted entities should be removed (hard-delete)
items.how: A delete removes the entity row and its payload. SQLite would otherwise leave the bytes in the file, so secure_delete is switched on for every connection, and a test looks inside the database file after a delete. Only a payload-free tombstone remains.

items.quote: while unpublish should still keep the data in your persistence layer.
items.how: An unPublish keeps the row and its payload and marks the entity unpublished. Users stop seeing it; admins still do, with a status block saying it is unpublished.

sections.title: 3. Data storage
sections.blurb: EF Core, a relational database, and the latest version.

items.quote: EF Core + Relational database of your choice.
items.how: EF Core on SQLite, with a single migration for the final schema applied at startup. SQLite keeps the demo self-contained; the design lists what a server database would need (a known limit, K1).

items.quote: Entities must keep track of the latest data version.
items.how: Each entity stores its version. A lower or equal version never overwrites it, and a concurrency token refuses a stale concurrent write so that attempt fails and retries.

live.label: Open a record and read its version

sections.title: 4. REST API
sections.blurb: Listing for consumers, the admin view, and the admin override.

items.quote: Provide endpoints that support listing entities for consumers.
items.how: GET /api/entities lists a page at a time by an opaque keyset cursor (default 50, at most 100) and GET /api/entities/{id} reads one. Both are read-only. A bad cursor is a 400.

items.quote: If the user is an admin (feel free to decide which userId/email corresponds to that of an admin), it will receive all entities that a normal user can see, including the ones that were disabled. No need to implement separate endpoints, feel free to decide how to approach this!
items.how: The same two endpoints serve both, and the caller's role decides what they see. Users see published entities that are not disabled; admins see everything, each with a status block. Which account is an admin is configuration: each user account has a Role. A hidden entity gives a user the same 404 as one that never existed.

live.label: Switch between user and admin views

items.quote: Data can not be updated by any kind of users,
items.how: No route updates, replaces or deletes an entity, for any role. A test lists every mapped write route, so a new one cannot appear unnoticed, and a PUT is refused for every caller.

live.label: See the PUT refused for every caller

items.quote: but an admin can disable them from the API - this will not affect the CMS, it’s an overwrite that does not affect CMS data!
items.how: Admins POST /api/entities/{id}/disable (and /enable). It changes only separate override columns: payload, version and published flag are untouched, CMS events never write the override, and a later publish does not clear it. Every use is audited with who did it.

sections.title: 5. Performance
sections.blurb: Asynchronous or synchronous, and why; the read-only and writer contexts; optimised reads.

items.quote: Feel free to use any asynchronous mechanisms to process incoming requests. This can also be synchronous, but we would like to understand why either decision was taken.
items.how: Durable asynchronous: accept validates and stores the batch in one transaction, answers 202, and a background worker applies it. DESIGN section 3 weighs three options (synchronous; in-memory asynchronous, which loses events in a crash; durable asynchronous) and says why: a webhook sender wants a quick answer and retries anything that is not 2xx, an acknowledgement must mean safely stored, and a burst becomes a visible, bounded queue. The cost is that 202 means stored, not applied, so the sender follows the batch.

live.label: See the event's life, step by step

items.quote: Use a read-only/writer configuration for your application context
items.how: Two EF contexts: a write context, and a read context that tracks nothing and is opened read-only at the connection (Mode=ReadOnly), so it cannot write even by mistake. WAL mode lets readers carry on beside the single writer.

items.quote: and optimize your EF read queries.
items.how: Reads project straight to a DTO, track nothing, use no Include, write the stored payload text raw and page by key so cost does not grow with depth. Tests assert the number of queries and read the query plan to prove the indexes are used; the worker reads entity state in two queries however large the batch.

sections.title: 6. Observability
sections.blurb: Logging what was processed, and what failed.

items.quote: Log processed events, including failing ones.
items.how: Every event is logged with batch id, position, entity id, type, version, outcome, reason and checksum, rejected and failing ones included, at a level that fits (stale and rejected are warnings). A correlation id ties the response header, every log line and the database rows together, and worker health, retries and set-aside batches are logged too. No payload, password or Authorization header is ever logged.

sections.title: 7. Testing
sections.blurb: How events are processed, the ingestion constraints, and basic authentication.

items.quote: Test how events are processed and whether the ingestion constraints are successfully followed by the service.
items.how: The suite runs the real HTTP pipeline against a real SQLite file per test class and checks rows with raw SQL. It has a test for every rule in the reconciliation table in both arrival orders, order independence against an independent oracle on random shuffles and on every permutation of curated timelines, and a pass and a fail input at every ingestion limit.

items.quote: Test your basic authentication mechanism with valid/invalid user-password combinations.
items.how: Valid and invalid combinations are tried for every account (CMS, user, admin): a right user with a wrong password, an unknown user, an empty password, malformed headers, other schemes, and the failed-sign-in throttle. Every role is also tried against every route in a role matrix.

live.label: Run the matrix and sign-in cases

sections.title: 8. Deliverable
sections.blurb: The solution, its README, cross-platform, and a repository. Two of these four are not fully met, and the matrix says so.

items.quote: .NET Core 9 or above solution.
items.how: A .NET 9 solution (net9.0) with RollForward set to Major, so it also runs where only a newer runtime is installed. .NET 9 leaves support on 10 November 2026; moving to net10.0 is a one-line change.

items.quote: Provide a README with setup/running instructions.
items.how: The README covers prerequisites, running, a try-it flow that includes following a batch, tests, configuration, running outside Development, the database and migrations, and the ranked limitations. Its try-it commands were run against the built service, and a CI job is written to run them on every push.

items.quote: The solution should work on either Mac or Windows, so build it platform-agnostic.
items.how: The code uses no OS-specific paths. A CI workflow builds and tests on Windows, macOS and Linux with warnings treated as errors. Windows and Ubuntu pass in CI, and the build, both test suites and a real-service smoke test also pass by hand on Debian 13 (linux-testing.md).
items.gap: macOS is not green: it passed on CI runs 1 and 2 and failed its Test step on run 3 (the latest), and the log has not been read, so the cause is unknown.

items.quote: Github repo with all the above.
items.how: Everything, with its history, is pushed to github.com/pahayward/LateralCMS, and CI runs on every push.

sections.title: The brief's own notes
sections.blurb: What it says it is judged on.

items.quote: Focus on the correctness, structure, and clarity of the system.
items.how: Correctness: a pure reducer checked against an independent oracle, and deliberate defects that each had to be caught by a named test. Structure: one web project with feature folders, the rules in a Domain folder that references nothing but the base library (a test enforces it), and an interface only where a second implementation is plausible. Clarity: a design document that gives each decision and its alternatives, a README that is run in CI, this requirements matrix kept true by a test, and this console.

items.quote: Correct event processing is the most important part.
items.how: The reducer is a pure function of the stored entity, the tombstone and one event, with deterministic ties, so the result never depends on arrival order or on how batches are split. The one assumption it needs (a higher version never carries an earlier timestamp) is stated, and its two counterexamples are pinned by tests that assert the divergence rather than hidden.

beyond.title: Beyond the brief
beyond.blurb: Things the user asked for afterwards, and how each was met.

items.quote: Payload checksum, e.g. MD5, stored with the object and returned to the publisher
items.how: Every validated publish and unPublish gets a checksum over its canonical text: SHA-256 by default, MD5 by setting, and self-describing (sha256:…). It is returned in the response, stored with the entity, served by the API and recorded in the ledger. A test recomputes it from the stored payload.

items.quote: Where payloads are stored; dependency injection of storage and database
items.how: Payloads sit inline in the entity row (up to 256 KiB). Dependencies are injected, with an interface only where a second implementation is plausible: the checksum, the clock, the asset store and the scanner. EF Core is not wrapped in a repository, so tests use the real database.

items.quote: A written set of design guidelines, used as an audit
items.how: docs/GUIDELINES.md holds the rules the code is held to, and they are numbered so a review can cite them.

items.quote: What if someone uploads a 10 GB video?
items.how: The webhook refuses a body by its declared length before reading a byte, and media is referenced from an event, never carried in it. The file itself then got its own path: the asset store, with multipart upload, scanning and ranged downloads.

items.quote: A test console, an endpoints tab, a one-click Visual Studio launch, a fenced test-only reset
items.how: The engineering console (this page) covers the test console and the endpoints, as the API workbench. The reset exists only where it was switched on and is refused in Production.
items.gap: The one-click Visual Studio launch profile was copied from the first build and has not been verified, because it needs Visual Studio.

items.quote: A line-by-line requirements matrix, a development story, generated diagrams
items.how: The requirements matrix is docs/REQUIREMENTS.md (every row with its tests, mutations and status) and this page. The diagrams are generated from one script and shown in the console, the README and DESIGN.
items.gap: There is no separate development-story document: the closest things are the rebuild brief, which records the plan and why, and the commit history.

items.quote: They are really looking for a robust async solution
items.how: One durable asynchronous pipeline from the start: nothing is acknowledged until it is stored, the worker applies batches with retries and back-off, a poisoned batch is set aside without blocking the others, takedowns are applied first and never given up on, and the queue is bounded and observable.

items.quote: Why not implement a local version supports multiple content sizes/allows parallel downloads of large assets ? Something which starts to close the gap between a local CMS and something like AWS S3?
items.how: A local S3-like asset store: single PUT up to a limit and S3-style multipart above it with parts sent in parallel and checksummed; downloads with Range, If-Range and ETag so many ranges of one large file are fetched at once; a quota; content-addressed storage so identical files are stored once; and physical deletion. The photo library keeps three sizes of every picture in it.

items.quote: would what's been produced be considered secure by design - where does it fail and where does it succeed. How might you close the gaps
items.how: A security review (DESIGN section 12) lists where it succeeds and where it is weak, ranked, with the fix for each. The gaps that were cheap to close were closed: no committed credentials, a bound on the memory a burst of senders can use, forwarded headers trusted only from named proxies, an allow-list for the reset, an append-only audit log, and a console that refuses to run outside Development. The rest are written down as limits.

items.quote: Consider mocking out a security scanner for the uploaded content - we don't want uploaded content to have any malicious payload
items.how: Every upload is quarantined and scanned by a mock behind an interface, so a real engine can replace it. Only a clean asset is ever served, a flagged one is wiped and keeps only its verdict, and a scanner that errors or times out fails closed. The mock is not malware protection; it proves the pipeline.

items.quote: a sample application which is more like an end user, consumer facing page for a photo library management system
items.how: A photo library that keeps everything in the CMS: photos are entities, pictures are scanned assets in three sizes, every edit is a new version, and it shows a timeline, albums, favourites, trash, search and parallel upload and download. Its console tests cover the read-only media route it needs.

items.quote: the engineering panel - it looks confusing to be honest at first sight and could do with an overhall
items.how: Rebuilt around what a tester does: an overview with a guided tour, a records explorer that drills into one record, an API workbench that shows any call as curl or PowerShell and runs it, and live checks. The architecture diagrams and the design documentation are in it, and a test keeps its endpoint catalogue equal to the service's real routes and roles.

items.quote: Login system, user admin, what's the admin password?, change the admin password & method to reset when on ssh
items.how: People now live in the database with salted PBKDF2 hashes. They sign in with a session cookie (or Basic credentials for scripts); an administrator adds, disables, re-roles, resets and deletes them in the engineering console; a temporary password must be replaced before anything else is allowed; a fresh install makes one administrator whose temporary password is in a private file, not the log; and the operator can reset any password over SSH with dotnet Lateral.Cms.dll admin set-password, with the service running or stopped.
items.gap: The photo library and the engineering console still act as fixed accounts read from a settings file, and only run in the Development environment on the loopback address, so they have no sign-in page of their own. People sign in to the CMS itself (session or Basic), and the administrator manages them in the engineering console.

items.quote: config options available in engineering / admin side
items.how: The administrator can read every setting the service has, with its value now, its default, whether it came from a file, an environment variable or the command line, the environment variable that sets it and what it is for. Secrets show only as set or not set. It is read-only on purpose: the service reads its configuration at start-up, so the page writes the lines to paste into the settings file or environment instead. A test fails if a setting exists without a description.

items.quote: where stuff is gonna get stored - storage options
items.how: A page and an endpoint say where everything is kept (one SQLite file, one folder of asset bytes, the session keys, and logs on standard output), how big each is, how much room the disks have, how much of the quota is used and what to back up. The paths are settings (Database:ConnectionString, Assets:Root, Assets:MaxBytes).
items.gap: There is one storage option for each: SQLite for records and the local file system for assets. The asset store is behind an interface so an S3-compatible backend could replace it, but none is built, and there is no built-in backup command.

items.quote: Assume I will put this into production and serve it as an app in it's own use on my home lab.
items.how: The CMS service is set up for it: no committed or default password, a first-run administrator, accounts and sessions, an SSH recovery command, visible settings and storage, a Production mode that refuses the reset route, and a written home-server guide (install folder, environment file, systemd unit, reverse proxy, backups, upgrades). The first-run, sign-in, forced password change and SSH reset steps were run for real against a Production-mode service on a spare port.
items.gap: Only run on Windows. The Linux and systemd steps are written but have not been run, and nothing has been run behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS. The photo library and engineering console are still a development tool (loopback only, fixed accounts), not something to put in front of the household.
